## Hooks and context injection

### Q: What hook events does base respond to?
**A:** Five: session-start, user-prompt-submit, pre-tool-use, post-tool-use, and stop. All of them dispatch through `base hook <EVENT>`, which Claude Code calls automatically at each point in a turn. **Do not trust `base help hook` on this** — its summary line names only three (session-start, post-tool-use, user-prompt-submit) and omits pre-tool-use and stop. That is a stale help string in the binary, not a missing feature; the dispatcher in `src/hook/mod.rs` has all five arms. Confirmed at v0.13.2.
<!-- v0.13.2 | verified: cli-help|source -->

### Q: Can another installer wire base's hooks without letting base edit settings.json?
**A:** Yes: `base hooks manifest` prints base's hook wiring as JSON for an installer outside base to consume. The object carries the path of the running binary and a `hooks` array with one item per event (`SessionStart`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`), each giving the `command` to run (`base hook <event>`) and the ready-made `entry` fragment in the shape Claude Code's `settings.json` expects. `base install` still wires `~/.claude/settings.json` itself; `hooks manifest` is the read-only export of the same table for tooling that owns that file. It prints nothing but JSON. The other `base hooks` subcommand is `show` (below).
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: cli-help|audit -->

### Q: What does the session-start hook inject?
**A:** A pipeline including: a graph-health warning if unhealthy, tier auto-compaction if bloated, clearing this session's own dedup state, domain sync, ingesting `paul.toml` projects, active/deferred state reconciliation, an operator profile block, an update banner, all signals (memory, active-awareness, pulse, flow-resurface, handoff, reminder, fork), the flow protocol block, extension status, a context-triggers cheat sheet, and relay inbox/task delivery. All of it is collected and printed once. Line 1 is a header with every count and the path of `.base/last-session-start.md`, which holds the untrimmed output; then the instruction block, DUE NOW, up to 10 lettered handoffs (newest first, one per project), the 3 newest forks, and PROJECTS, TASKS and MILESTONES. Those three count every working item and list only what is on a project touched in the last `[session_start] recent_project_days` days (7): that is what "in progress" means there, since no task status says it. Everything else follows, and if the output is over `[budget] session_start_bytes` (10000) the bottom blocks shrink to one line each, naming the command or the file that holds the rest.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: What does the user-prompt-submit hook do?
**A:** It increments the prompt count and derives the current bracket (FRESH/MODERATE/DEPLETED/CRITICAL), builds the bracket rules, then checks for a star command. If a star command matched, it short-circuits everything else for that prompt. Otherwise it syncs domains, loads the merged graph, gathers active file paths, matches domains, builds rules and context per matched domain and the walk's `<base-context>` blocks, and finally adds the relay inbox, tasks and wake contract. Everything is a named block with a priority: (1) rules matched to the prompt, star-command output and topic rules; (2) a matched domain's CONTEXT and query, and the walk; (3) relay, the wake contract last; (4) always-on domains, `always` rules and grounding; (5) bracket rules, then DEVMODE. The `<context-bracket>` line always goes first and names the tier on every prompt. Each bracket rule is sent once per session, on the first prompt where its tier applies, never again (a tier change sends only the new tier's rules), and not at all when its `covered_by` text is in a CLAUDE.md Claude Code loads (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, or `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md` or `CLAUDE.local.md` in the working folder or above it). A decision of an always-on domain such as GLOBAL is in the prompt's CONTEXT only when the prompt contains one of its keywords (`base decision update <slug> --keywords "..."`); one with no keywords is shown at session start only. Over `[budget] prompt_bytes` (10000), whole blocks are dropped lowest priority first, and a dropped lower block comes back if it fits the room left; each dropped block leaves one line naming it, its size and `base hooks show <block>`. A block is never cut, and a rule counts as shown only if its block was printed, so a dropped rule is sent on a later prompt. `.base/hook-output.jsonl` records every dropped block by name, items and bytes, and `base doctor` names them.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: The prompt hook said it withheld a block. How do I read it?
**A:** Run the command on the pointer line: `base hooks show <block>`, for example `base hooks show relay-wake`. It prints that block exactly as the hook built it, from this session's own file `.base/hook-output/<session id>/prompt-blocks.json` (the session is `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`, or `--session <id>`), so another session's prompt in the same workspace never answers for yours. With no block named it lists the last prompt's blocks with their priority, size, and whether each was printed or withheld. It reads what the hook kept and changes nothing; relay messages in a dropped block were already consumed when they were delivered, so this is the only place their text still is. The file holds the session's last prompt only and is removed after 7 days.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: How do I see what a prompt or a file touch matched, and why a rule was or was not served?
**A:** Run `base log matches`. Every prompt, and every tool call that touches a file, appends one row to `.base/match-log.jsonl` (the workspace's `.base`, else the global tier's): which domains matched and by what (`always`, the `keyword` that hit, the `path` folder or trigger that held the file, `parent` for a nested parent, `file_keyword`), each rule and decision served by id and the block that carried it, each one cut with its reason (`budget` under `prompt_bytes` or `walk_budget`, `topic limit` under `[rules] topic_max`, `not matched` under `topic_min_score`), and the topic scores. `base log matches` prints the last 20 rows, one line each: time, event, each domain and what matched it, how many were served and cut, and the prompt's start or the file. `--last <n>` sets how many, `--session <id>` and `--rule <id>` keep the rows of one session or one rule or decision (an id or its start), and `--json` prints the rows themselves. A prompt that matched only `GLOBAL(always)` is a keyword gap on record. The row is written after the hook's output is printed and never changes it. The log stays on the machine; secrets in a prompt (API keys, tokens, `password=` values, private keys, JWTs) are written as `[SECRET:<kind>]`. `[log] prompt_text` keeps the whole prompt (`full`, the default), only the words that matched (`matched`), or none (`off`), and session start removes rows older than `[log] prompt_days` (90): once a day it moves the log of earlier days to `.base/match-log/` and deletes the files there whose rows have all aged out, so the log being written is never rewritten.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: How do I know my domain keywords fire on the prompts they are meant for, and stay quiet on the rest?
**A:** Give the rules test prompts and run `base rule test`. A rule carries up to 3 prompts that must serve it (`--fires-on`) and up to 2 that must not (`--quiet-on`): pass them to `base rule add`, or add them to an existing rule with `base rule update <domain>.<id>`, taking the id from `base rule list --domain <domain>` (`[base.9f2c1a7b]`). They are stored with the rule: on its `domains.toml` entry (as `fires_on` and `quiet_on`), or on its graph record for a rule `base rule add` wrote; `--clear-tests` empties both lists first. `base rule test` (or `--domain X`, or `--rule <domain>.<id>`) runs every stored prompt through the prompt hook's own matching, as the first prompt of a fresh session: a star command passes every rule by; a rule with matchers of its own is served on its score, as the hook serves it; any other rule is served when its domain comes in (always-on, or a prompt keyword as whole words, with `exclude` and `auto_inject = false` honoured). It prints a passing rule on one line and a failing rule with every prompt, and under each `MISS` (a fires-on prompt that did not serve the rule) or `FALSE FIRE` (a quiet-on prompt that did) one `matched:` line saying what came in and why the rule's domain did not (`base: has no prompt keywords`, `no keyword matched`, `excluded by "..."`). With BM25 on (`[match] bm25`, the default), each prompt's line ends with its BM25 score, a fires-on prompt held out of its own rule's text, and one line above the totals says how they were judged: with `[match] min_score` unset (the default) by keyword only, with it set a rule no keyword brings is served at that score. Then the totals and how many rules in each domain have no tests. It exits 1 on any miss or false fire, 0 otherwise, and 2 when it cannot run (an unknown domain or rule). The prompt budget and the session's dedup are not replayed: the test is of the config. After `base domain add-trigger`, `remove-trigger`, `create`, `remove`, `paths --apply` and `base rule add` or `update`, one line gives the domain's test result when it has tests.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: Which of my rules never fire, fire on almost every prompt, or get ignored?
**A:** Run `base doctor` and read its section `rules and decisions, from the match log`, then `base rule stats` for every rule's numbers. Both read `.base/match-log.jsonl` (your workspace's and the global tier's) and count a rule as served only where the prompt hook printed it whole: a rule cut for the budget, or only scored, is not served. **Dead**: an injecting rule not served in `[doctor] dead_days` days (30). A domain that matched nothing in that time is one line for all its rules; a rule that was only ever withheld by the budget names the block (`base hooks show <block>`); a rule never seen in the log since its domain last matched is counted as too new, not listed. **Noisy**: a domain matched by keyword on more than `[tune] broad_share` (25%) of the prompts you typed in that time, counting only keywords it still has, so narrowing one clears the line at once; path matches and task notifications do not count, it is judged once 100 typed prompts are logged, and not at all under `[log] prompt_text = "matched"` or `"off"` (a row then keeps too little to tell your prompt from a task notification). A global decision with keywords is judged the same way; a rule with matchers of its own is not. **Ignored**: a rule or decision served and then corrected at least `[doctor] ignored_after` times (3), and after at least twice the log's average share of servings (its line prints both shares: about 1 in 6 servings is followed by some correction, so a rule must be corrected after 1 in 3 of its own to stand out), the correction about the reply the rule was served for or the next one: a phrase (C1), a repeated request or a `UPDATED:` / `CORRECTED:` marker (C3) on the following prompt, or an interrupt, a refused tool call or a file of yours the AI wrote and you changed (C2) in that turn. A phrase on the prompt that brought the rule in is about the reply before it and does not count; a reworded rule is a new rule and starts at 0. **Review**: a decision served `[doctor] review_served` times (20) with no `base decision update` for `[doctor] review_days` days (60), asking "still true?". The last line is the correction detector's record from `base tune`'s passes in the same window. While the log covers fewer days than `dead_days`, the dead list says how many days it covers instead of calling every rule dead; that age is your workspace's own log, so a workspace first used yesterday is one day old. All of it is advice: it never changes doctor's verdict. `base rule stats [--domain X] [--json]` prints, per rule, times served in the last `dead_days` days and in all, times a correction followed, and the day it was last served.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: How do I try a different matcher, or pending rule proposals, without changing what my sessions are served?
**A:** Start a shadow. `base shadow start --matcher bm25` (or `keyword-only`, with any of `--min-score X`, `--prompt-idf`, `--min-terms N`, `--relative R`) runs that matcher as a candidate beside the live one; `base shadow start --from-proposals p-0001,p-0002` runs pending proposals as the candidate, applied in memory. Every prompt and file touch then runs both, only live's pick is served, and each match-log row records what the candidate would have added or dropped (`shadow`), in milliseconds; a run past `[shadow] max_ms` (50) is stopped and logged as skipped. `base shadow report` shows the events, where the two differ, and the wins and losses: a correction about a reply (sorted to the rule it fits, as `base rule propose` sorts one) is a win when the candidate would have served that rule and live did not, a loss when live served it and the candidate would not have. At session start a candidate is promoted once it has run on `[shadow] min_prompts` (200) typed prompts, its wins are at least `[shadow] win_ratio` (3) times its losses (zero losses count as one, so it needs 3 wins), and no loss is on a rule marked protected (`base rule update <domain>.<id> --protected`). Promotion writes the candidate's `[match]` keys into `~/.base-gbl/base.toml`, line by line and after a backup (`base.toml.BAK-<date>-pre-<version>`), or approves its proposals; session start says so once, with `base shadow rollback` to undo it. `[shadow] auto_promote = false` asks instead: session start says once that it is ready, and `base shadow promote` does it. After a promotion, once `[shadow] watch_prompts` (100) typed prompts have passed, corrections per 100 are compared with the 100 before; a rise past `[shadow] rollback_sd` (2.5) times the chance variation at the earlier rate rolls it back on its own (about 15 per 100 at 24 corrections per 100). `base shadow promote`, `rollback` and `stop` always work by hand. With no shadow started nothing changes: no session-start line, no `shadow` field.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: How does base notice that I corrected the AI?
**A:** Four checks, and no one of them decides. (1) Wording: each prompt you type after a session's first is checked for a phrase from `[corrections] phrases`, as whole words with case ignored (the defaults: "no,", "wrong", "that's not", "not what i asked", "i told you", "i've said", "i said", "again", "quit", "stop doing", "don't", "never", "why did you", and swearing). (2) What you did: you stopped a turn with Esc, refused a tool call, changed a file the AI wrote after its turn ended, or sent nearly the same request twice in a row (half or more of the content words shared, `[corrections] repeat_similarity`). Claude Code runs no Stop hook after an Esc or a refusal, so the prompt hook reads that turn when your next prompt arrives; every transcript line is read once. (3) The AI's own marker at the start of a line of its reply: `CORRECTED:`, `UPDATED:`, `MISREAD:` or `DEFERRED:` (`[corrections] markers`). A marker in backticks, in a code block or in the middle of a line is a quote, and text in CLAUDE.md, hook output, a reminder or a tool result is never the AI's reply, so none of those count. (4) When (1) fires on a prompt, or a signal from (2) is waiting, that prompt carries one line: `This may be a correction. If it is, run base rule propose --from-turn after answering.` The AI, which read the whole exchange, decides. A task notification never carries the line; the signal waits for your next prompt. Every flag is a row in the match log (`event: "signal"`). `base log corrections` prints this session's rows (`--session <id>` another session's), and `base log corrections --transcript <path>` runs the same checks over a whole transcript, turn by turn, where a changed file is read from Claude Code's own note of it instead. `[corrections] enabled = false` turns all of it off.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: What does `base rule propose` do with a correction?
**A:** It turns one correction into a pending rule proposal. Inside Claude Code, `base rule propose --from-turn` reads the session's own transcript: the last prompt you typed, the marker line the AI wrote, and the signals of that turn and the one before it. It scores the correction against every rule and decision base holds (BM25 word scores); a record fits only when it scores at least twice the next one, since a long prompt shares a few words with many records. Then it sorts the correction three ways. A record fits and was served to this session up to that prompt: **rewrite**, the AI had the rule and broke it anyway (`--text` is the new wording). A record fits and was never served: **keyword gap**, its triggers missed; the keywords go on the rule's own words, the decision's keywords, or its domain. Nothing fits: **new rule**, which needs `--text`. `--keywords "a, b"` names the words that should bring it back (otherwise up to five are suggested from the prompt), and `--example "<prompt>"` the prompt it must fire on (otherwise yours); that prompt becomes its first `fires_on` test. `--rule <domain>.<id>`, `--decision <slug>` or `--new` overrides the sort, `--domain X` places a new rule, and running it again for the same turn replaces that turn's proposal and keeps its id. `--dry-run` prints the proposal and writes nothing; `--transcript <path> --prompt <n>` reads a past turn (the n-th prompt a person typed). A turn whose only marker is `DEFERRED:` (the AI held its position) is refused: a disagreement is logged, never proposed. The proposal is kept in the graph as pending, with the prompt, the marker line, the signals and the three closest records. Without `--from-turn` it needs `--example` and `--text` or `--keywords`.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: How do I check what a rule proposal would change before I approve it?
**A:** `base rule replay p-0007` runs the proposal over your last 500 prompts in the match log (`[tune] replay_prompts`), each judged twice as the first prompt of a fresh session: once on today's config and once with the change made. It prints how many prompts it replayed and from when, the prompts that would newly serve the rule, the prompts that would stop, and the share of all replayed prompts that would serve it after the change. A change served on more than `[tune] broad_share` (25%) of them, where the change adds at least one, is flagged `TOO BROAD`. What is judged follows the target: a domain is served when it matches, a rule as `base rule test` judges it, a decision of an always-on domain on its own keywords. Task notifications and rows logged with no text are left out and counted. Without a proposal, `base rule replay --domain X --add-keyword "..."` (or `--drop-keyword`, `--rule <domain>.<id>`, `--decision <slug>`) checks a change of your own.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: How do I approve, edit or reject rule proposals?
**A:** Session start shows `rule proposals: 3 pending · base rule review` after HANDOFFS when any are waiting; they are kept in the graph, so they are the ones left from earlier sessions. `base rule review` on a terminal shows each one with the prompt behind it, the AI's marker line, the signals and its replay, then takes one key: `a` approve, `e` edit (new wording and keywords, Enter keeps each, then its replay and `a` to apply), `r` reject, `s` skip, `q` stop. Without a terminal it lists them and changes nothing. For the AI acting for you: `--approve <id>`, `--reject <id> [--reason "..."]`, `--edit <id> --text "..." --keywords "a, b"`; a TOO BROAD change is refused unless `--broad-ok` is given. Approving a keyword gap adds the keywords to the domain's `domains.toml`, the rule's own words or the decision's keywords; a new rule is written with its keywords as its words and its prompt as its first `fires_on` test; a rewrite writes the new wording as a new rule (or decision) that supersedes the old one, which `base rule list --include-superseded` still shows. A rule from `domains.toml` moves to the graph to be rewritten, and the output says so. A rejected proposal is never proposed again.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: What does `base tune` do, and when should it run?
**A:** `base tune` is the rule pass: it reads what your sessions did since the last pass and writes rule proposals for `base rule review`. It applies nothing. For each session it reads the transcript turn by turn, only past the turns the last pass judged, and makes one Haiku call (headless Claude Code on `claude-haiku-4-5`, loading no settings, MCP servers or tools, with base's own hooks off) that says which typed prompts corrected the AI, the one-sentence rule that would have prevented each, and which domain a prompt that matched none belongs to. A judged correction is sorted the way `base rule propose` sorts one (keyword gap, rewrite or new rule), with the judge's wording and keywords; prompts that matched no domain become a keyword gap on the domain the judge names. Once a day, or with `--store`, one more call reads the match log for rules to merge (served together, overlapping wording), rules to split (one rule holding two instructions) and keywords to drop (a keyword that brings its domain onto prompts not about it, with narrower words in its place). A rule nothing served in a match log 30 days long, and that the pass has known for 30 days (a rule added or re-worded since is too new), is proposed for retirement with no call. Answers are cached by content hash as they arrive, so a rerun on the same turns makes no call, and `--max-calls <n>` (10 by default) caps a pass; sessions past it wait for the next one. A call takes about a minute, so a pass can run for several minutes: run it in the background when your shell stops commands after a couple of minutes, and a stopped pass loses nothing it was already told. A session whose only typed prompt is its first one (a spawned session's boot prompt) matched a domain and holds no correction, so it is read with no call. A correction base's detector did not flag is saved as a detector test case in `~/.base-gbl/corrections/tune/missed-cases.json`, on your machine only. It reads the session running it (its last turn left out), sessions that ended or sat untouched for a day with turns no pass has read, and other live sessions only when a pass is due for them; `--session <id>` and `--transcript <path>` (each repeatable) name sessions instead. `base tune --dry-run` shows what it would read and how many calls it would make, and calls nothing. You do not have to remember it: after `[tune] corrections` (3) flagged corrections since the last pass, the next prompt carries `rule pass due: 3 corrections since the last one · run base tune`; after `[tune] turns` (15) typed prompts with at least one flagged correction or one prompt that matched no domain, `rule pass due: 15 prompts since the last one · run base tune`. The line shows once, and again only after another `[tune] turns` prompts with no pass. Session start shows `rule pass due: 2 earlier sessions have unreviewed corrections · run base tune` for sessions that ended, or were left open a day, with corrections no pass has read. The SessionEnd hook (`base hook session-end`) only marks the session ended, since most sessions are closed without one. No hook calls the model: the AI runs `base tune` as a command. `[tune] corrections = 0` or `turns = 0` turns that trigger off, and `[corrections] enabled = false` turns off the counting and both lines.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: What do merge, split, retire and drop-keyword proposals change when I approve them?
**A:** They come from `base tune`'s once-a-day store check and go through `base rule review` like the others, each with its replay. **Drop keyword** takes the keyword off the domain, rule or decision and adds the narrower words the judge gave, in one approval. **Merge** writes one new rule with the merged wording, in the first rule's domain and tier, carrying both rules' keywords and tests, and it supersedes both. **Split** rewrites the rule as its first part (the old wording is superseded) and adds the second part as a new rule beside it. **Retire** stops the rule being served by any hook and deletes nothing: the rule keeps its text, gets the status `retired`, and still shows in `base rule list --include-superseded`; `base rule unretire <domain>.<id>` serves it again. A rule from `domains.toml` moves to the graph first, as a rewrite does, and the output says so. Old superseded wording stays listed the same way.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: Why does base offer to add a CORRECTED line to my CLAUDE.md?
**A:** So the AI marks its own corrections, the clearest of the four signals base reads. The line is `When the user corrects you, start that reply with "CORRECTED: <what you got wrong>".` `base install` and `base scaffold` ask once, on a terminal, when your `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` does not already ask for `CORRECTED:` or `UPDATED:`. Yes puts the line there just above the `## BASE CLI` section. For an unattended install, `base install --corrections-line` adds it and `base install --no-corrections-line` does not. The answer is kept in `~/.base-gbl/.corrections-line`. If you said no, or were never asked, session start carries the same line once per session, unless a CLAUDE.md the session loads (yours, the project's or a managed one) asks for one of those markers. `base uninstall` removes the line with the BASE CLI section.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: Claude Code updated and `base doctor` says to re-measure. What does `base doctor --measure` do?
**A:** It measures how much hook text the running Claude Code actually delivers to the model, for session start, prompt submit and pre-tool, and sets the budgets from it. For each hook it runs headless `claude -p` calls on Haiku, each loading one temporary hook (and none of your own) that prints a payload of a known size with numbered marker lines, and asks the model which markers it saw and whether it saw the end line. Sizes double from 4,000 bytes until one is cut, then the gap is halved down to 500 bytes: about 7 calls per hook, never more than 12. It prints every probe, then writes `session_start_bytes`, `prompt_bytes`, `pre_tool_bytes` and `measured_on` to `~/.base-gbl/base.toml`, keeping every other line and comment, and prints each value before and after. If any hook fails to measure, nothing is written. `base doctor` compares `measured_on` with the running Claude Code and, when they differ, says `run base doctor --measure`. On Claude Code 2.1.287 every hook delivered 10,000 bytes whole and handed 10,500 over as a 2,000-character preview, so the shipped defaults are 10,000.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: What does the pre-tool-use hook do?
**A:** It injects the AST file map for source files being touched, intercepts grep-style commands (`grep -r`, `rg`, `ag`, `ack`, `fd`, `find -name`, piped `grep`) with an `<ast-hint>` block nudging you toward `base ast query`, injects domain rules for matched paths, applies a markdown-frontmatter contract on Write/Edit of `.md` files, applies MIDAS standards on mutating operations, delivers mid-turn relay tasks/pings, and marks the current app "dirty" on any Edit/Write/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit so the Stop hook knows to refresh its AST map.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source -->

### Q: What does the post-tool-use hook do?
**A:** It updates internal timestamps and injects section-specific AST context for partial file reads, i.e. context about the exact lines you just read, not the whole file.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source -->

### Q: What does the stop hook do?
**A:** It spawns a detached `base sync --ast --target <app>` for the cwd app plus every app that was dirtied (edited) during the turn. This only applies to apps that already have a `.base-ast/ast.ttl` map (opt-in), is debounced 20 seconds, and is never awaited, so it doesn't block your session ending.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source -->

### Q: How does pre-tool-use injection actually reach Claude, mechanically?
**A:** Differently from the other hooks. Session-start, user-prompt-submit, and stop write plain stdout, which Claude Code prepends directly into context. Pre-tool-use must instead use a JSON envelope, `{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","additionalContext":"..."}}`, because plain stdout on that event is transcript-only and never reaches the model.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source|reference -->

### Q: What actually controls whether something gets injected into my session?
**A:** A layered system: (1) domain matching against prompt keywords, file keywords, and active file paths, deterministic substring/path matching, nothing fuzzy or semantic, and never context-size-aware; (2) suppression, each signal's output is hashed and unchanged output is skipped, so silence is the default steady state; (3) a size budget, `[budget] session_start_bytes` (default 10000, counted in bytes, which is what the host counts, and measured on the host by `base doctor --measure`), over everything session start prints: nothing is exempt, blocks at the bottom shrink to one line naming where the rest is, and the old `signal.max_chars` is read by nothing (`base doctor --fix` moves it to `[budget] memory_chars` when that is unset, or removes it); the memory block also has its own budget inside that one, `[budget] memory_chars` (default 4000), filled with whole notes, corrections first and newest first, then one line counting the rest and naming `base learn --list`; handoffs, reminders and forks are still exempt from suppression and surface every session until acted on; (4) the bracket system layering rule-injection intensity on top of session depletion. Layers 1 to 3 are purely trigger- and content-based. Layer 4 is the exception: in percent mode (what `base install` writes by default) the bracket reads real context depletion from the live transcript's usage block, so injection volume does adapt to how full your context window is. See the bracket pair below for the tiers and thresholds.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: Does base take the size of my current context window into account when deciding what to load?
**A:** Partly yes, through the bracket system. WHAT matches is never context-aware: domains fire on keyword/path matches against the prompt and recently-active files, with no regard for how full your context is. But HOW MUCH gets injected is context-aware when brackets run in percent mode, which is what current installs get: `base install` writes `bracket.mode = "percent"` into `base.toml`, and in that mode base reads the live Claude Code transcript's most recent `usage` block (summing `input_tokens` + `cache_read_input_tokens` + `cache_creation_input_tokens`) and divides by `bracket.context_window` (default 200000) to compute real depletion. That percentage picks the tier: FRESH at or below `fresh_until_pct` (default 20), MODERATE to 45, DEPLETED to 70, CRITICAL above. If `mode` is absent (a `base.toml` predating the feature) or the transcript has no usage yet, it falls back to counting prompts (`fresh_until` 3, `moderate_until` 10, `depleted_until` 20). So the bracket is a genuine live read of context depletion on a modern install, and a turn-count proxy only on legacy config or first prompt. It governs injection volume and dedup frequency, not whether injection happens at all.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source -->

### Q: What are "brackets" and why do I see the same rules every prompt?
**A:** Brackets are a depletion-staging system configured under `[bracket]` in `base.toml` that tracks how deep you are into a session: FRESH (lean injection, e.g. skipping the graph neighborhood), MODERATE (full injection), then DEPLETED and CRITICAL (force-refresh dedup more often, on `refresh_interval`, default every 5 prompts). Which tier you are in depends on `bracket.mode`. In `"percent"` mode (what `base install` writes for new installs) base reads real context depletion from the live transcript and compares it to `fresh_until_pct` / `moderate_until_pct` / `depleted_until_pct` (defaults 20 / 45 / 70 percent of `context_window`, default 200000). When `mode` is absent or the transcript has no usage block yet, it falls back to prompt counts (`fresh_until` 3, `moderate_until` 10, `depleted_until` 20). Brackets govern how much and how often rules get re-injected, not what content matches your prompt. Bracket-tier rules are intentionally never deduplicated, they reinject every single prompt, on purpose, so your most critical standing rules don't quietly erode as the conversation fills up. The `always` bucket fires at every tier and is additive with the tier-specific bucket. They are also built before the star-command check, so they still fire even when a star command is active.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source -->

### Q: How do I preview what base would inject for a given prompt, without actually submitting it?
**A:** `base context "<some prompt text>"` runs the exact same matching engine the session-start and prompt-submit hooks use, matching your text against configured domain triggers and printing whatever would have been injected. It's read-only and doesn't affect session state.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I see every trigger base currently has configured?
**A:** `base context --list` lists all available context triggers across domains without matching against any text, showing which domains exist and what keywords or paths would fire them (empty if a domain has no keywords configured, e.g. a global rules-only domain).
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: Why does base sometimes say nothing at session start? Is it broken?
**A:** Probably not, silence is the intended steady state once your setup is healthy and stable. Each signal's output is hashed and unchanged output is suppressed so you're not re-shown the same thing every session. Things that always surface regardless are open handoffs, due reminders, and open forks. If you have none of those and nothing changed, getting no output is correct behavior, not a failure. Verify with `base doctor` and, if you want to confirm hooks are actually firing, tail `hook-events.jsonl` in the workspace `.base/` folder, which logs `domains_matched` and `rules_injected` per hook event.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source|reference -->

### Q: A hook doesn't seem to be injecting anything. How do I debug it?
**A:** Run the hook manually and read stderr, since hooks are fail-open and print errors only there. For example: `echo '{"prompt":"test message"}' | base hook user-prompt-submit`. If nothing prints to stdout and nothing useful is on stderr, the hook likely ran cleanly and simply had nothing to inject.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source|audit -->

### Q: What example JSON do I feed a hook to test it manually?
**A:** It depends on the event. For user-prompt-submit: `echo '{"prompt":"your test text"}' | base hook user-prompt-submit`. For session-start you typically don't need a payload: `echo '{}' | base hook session-start`. The point is to bypass Claude Code entirely and see the hook's stdout/stderr directly.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source -->

### Q: What does base's "fail-open" hook design actually mean, and why does it matter for debugging?
**A:** Every hook error is caught, printed to stderr only, and the process exits 0 with empty stdout, so a broken hook is indistinguishable from a hook that legitimately had nothing to say. This is deliberate: a broken graph or crashed extraction should never block your session. The consequence is that Claude Code typically doesn't surface hook stderr, so silent breakage can persist for a long time unnoticed. The fix is to run the hook manually via stdin JSON and inspect stderr directly, or check `hook-events.jsonl`, rather than trying to infer failure from missing output.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source|audit -->

### Q: hook-events.jsonl keeps growing. Is that a problem?
**A:** It's an append-only audit log of every hook firing (timestamp, hook name, success, domains matched, rules injected, suppressed, ast_injected, grep_intercepted) written under `~/.base-gbl/` and, for workspaces, also under `{workspace}/.base/`. It has no working rotation as of v0.12.3, so it grows unbounded; on a machine that's used base for a while it can reach several megabytes. A `rotate_hook_log` function does exist in the dashboard module (truncate above 10 MB, keep the last 5000 lines), but nothing in the codebase calls it, so it is dead code and never runs. It's useful as a diagnosis tool (grep it for `"success":false` or a specific hook name) but currently needs manual cleanup if disk usage becomes a concern.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source|audit -->

### Q: Even the audit log write itself can fail silently?
**A:** Yes, `log_hook_event` is fire-and-forget: if the write fails, nothing surfaces anywhere. It's one of several places in the codebase where fail-open means a broken write is simply invisible, consistent with the overall philosophy of never letting logging block a session.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source|audit -->

---

## Session relay

### Q: What is base relay for?
**A:** Session-to-session messaging between live Claude Code sessions, letting one session hand work to, or ping, another session that's currently open, without you manually copy-pasting context between terminals. It's built for parallel workers on the same or related projects.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I set up two sessions to talk to each other?
**A:** Both sessions need a registered title first: `base relay register --as <title>` in each one (`base relay init` creates the ephemeral relay store for a project if you need it). Confirm both are visible with `base relay sessions`. Then from session A: `*task <title-of-B> <what to do>` for real work, or `*ping <title-of-B> <message>` for a quick question. Without a registered title, a session can't receive relayed work and can't be addressed by name.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: reference|cli-help -->

### Q: What are the relay "codenames" I keep seeing, and why do they matter?
**A:** Sessions register under a friendly title via `base relay register --as <codename>` (often an animal name). That title is how `*task`/`*ping` address a specific live session, and it's how the current session's own identity gets resolved: matching the session's row in `base relay sessions` against `$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` answers "who am I" for handoff and relay purposes.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source|reference -->

### Q: What's the difference between *task, *ping, and *inbox?
**A:** All three relay messages between two *live* Claude Code sessions that each have a registered title, and all three are real star commands (confirmed via `base commands show task` / `base commands show ping`). `*task <title> <what to do>` packages real work into a briefing doc and relays it via `base relay task`, dropping it into another session's inbox; that session picks it up and works it autonomously via its own hooks, no further input from you. `*ping <title> <message>` is a same-turn instant message sent via `base relay ping`, no doc, no ceremony, for something like "is the auth guard rebuilt yet?", pausing in-flight work just long enough to send. `*inbox` is what the *receiving* session runs to read a pending ping (pings arrive on its next prompt, or at once through its inbox watcher) and reply to clear it. Both `*task` and `*ping` resolve an ambiguous or missing target by running `base relay sessions` first.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I send work from one session to another at the CLI level?
**A:** Both sessions need a registered title first (`base relay register --as <title>`). Then from the sending session run `base relay task --to "<title>" --slug "<kebab-case-slug>" --summary "<one-line summary>" --doc "<absolute-path-to-briefing-doc>" --priority high`. This drops the task into the target session's inbox, addressed to the session that holds the title now; it is shown in full on that session's next prompt or session start, working cross-workspace via the global tier. A new session that later takes the title is not shown it: the task is archived with the old session's inbox (see the question on codenames passing to a new session). Verify with `base relay tasks`, and the receiver clears it with `base relay done <slug>`.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help|source -->

### Q: What happens to my pings when a codename passes to a new session?
**A:** They stay with the session they were sent to. Every ping, task and notify records the session id that held the title when it was sent (`to_session`), and a session is only ever shown what was sent to it. When a title passes to another session (a restart, a `/clear` in the same tab, a codename handed out again, or another session running `base relay register --as <title>`), the previous holder's items move to `~/.base-gbl/.base/relay-inbox/.archive/<title>-<old session id>/`, so the new holder starts with an empty inbox. The sender of anything the previous holder was never shown gets one `relay: not delivered` notice in its own inbox, saying whose the title was, who holds it now and where the items are, so it can re-send what still applies. The notice goes to the session that sent the items, and only while it still holds its title; when base cannot tell which session sent an item (one written before this was built), nobody is told and the archive keeps it. A ping nobody was shown within a day is archived the same way. `~/.base-gbl/.base/title-history.jsonl` records which session held each title from when, which is how an item with no session id is placed.
<!-- v0.15.2 | verified: source -->

### Q: What's the difference between base relay task and base relay ping?
**A:** `task` is for heavier, briefed work: it requires a written doc, a slug, and an explicit `done` to clear it, and keeps firing until picked up. `ping` is an instant message with no doc and no done-ceremony: `base relay ping --to "<title>" --msg "<short message>"`, meant for quick questions. A ping is shown once, on the receiver's next prompt, as information: who sent it, when, the message and the reply command. While it stays unanswered, session start lists it in one line; replying with a ping is what clears it. If one sender sends again before the receiver's next prompt, only the newest is shown, with a line naming `base relay tasks --from <sender>`, which still lists the older ones.
<!-- v0.15.2 | verified: source -->

### Q: How does a receiving session clear a task or ping?
**A:** For a relayed task, the receiver runs `base relay done <slug>` once finished (and should note completion in its own state docs per the task's Definition of Done); this clears the inbox alert and closes the graph mirror of that task so it stops re-firing. For a ping, the receiver replies with `base relay ping --to <sender> --from <your-title> --msg "..."`, and that reply clears every ping from that sender, along with that sender's older relay messages; an unanswered ping stays listed in one line at each session start.
<!-- v0.15.2 | verified: source -->

### Q: I sent a ping or task but the other session doesn't seem to have gotten it. Why?
**A:** Delivery happens through hooks at the receiving session's next prompt or session start, never on a tool call, so a session that is idle, or deep in one long turn, sees a waiting message only when its inbox watcher wakes it. The watcher is the background Monitor that `base relay arm` prints; a session without one sees the message on its next prompt. A run that cannot keep a watcher at all (an Agent SDK run, a worker with no Monitor tool) sets `BASE_NO_WAKE_NUDGE`, and then each new message reaches it once, on its next tool call. Also note that `base relay poll` and `base relay board` are workspace-scoped, while `relay task`/`relay ping` route through the *global* session registry, so "No relay stores exist" from `poll`/`board` is not proof the message never arrived. `base relay sessions` showing the sender as live is the more trustworthy signal than an empty board. And if the receiver's title passed to another session before it read the message, the message was archived instead of delivered, and you were sent a `relay: not delivered` notice naming where it is.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source|reference -->

### Q: How do I see what relay sessions and activity exist right now?
**A:** `base relay board` gives the operator's view: sessions, liveness, claims, and pending messages, scoped to the current workspace (add `--project` to scope further). `base relay sessions` lists titled sessions in the global registry, which is what `*task`/`*ping` targets resolve against.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I see inbound relay tasks addressed to any live session?
**A:** `base relay tasks` lists inbound relay tasks across all live sessions. Use it right after sending a `relay task` to confirm the entry shows up with status pending.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: What message types does base relay send support?
**A:** `base relay send --to <TO> --type <TYPE> --msg <MSG>` supports types `claim`, `release`, `notify`, `unblock`, `contract-change`, `ready-to-merge`, `question`, `answer`. `--to` accepts a title, a session-id, `phase:<n>`, or `all`. This is the lower-level primitive that `task`/`ping` build convenience on top of.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->


### Q: How do I make one session wait for another instead of polling?
**A:** `base relay wait` blocks until a matching message arrives and burns zero session tokens while it waits. That is the whole point: a polling loop costs a tool call and context on every tick, while `wait` costs nothing until something actually lands. Narrow what it wakes for with `--from <sender>`, `--type <type>`, and `--project <project>`, and bound it with `--timeout <seconds>` (default 300). `--for <title>` lets you wait as a specific title instead of the session's own identity.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: Two sessions are about to edit the same files. How do I stop them colliding?
**A:** Advisory claims. `base relay claim <resource> [--note "..."] [--ttl <seconds>]` takes a TTL-bounded claim on a path or a phase (default TTL 3600 seconds), and `base relay release <resource>` gives it back. Claims show up in `base relay board`, so the other session, and you, can see who holds what. "Advisory" is the load-bearing word: nothing enforces a claim at the filesystem level, it is a coordination signal that cooperating sessions are expected to check. That is also why the TTL exists, so a session that dies never blocks a resource forever. An operator can break a stuck claim with `base relay release <resource> --force`.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I snapshot relay traffic, and how do I tear the store down when the work is done?
**A:** `base relay export` writes the spool out as `inbox.nq`, a read-only graph snapshot, when you want a durable record of what was relayed. `base relay dispose --project <project>` is the end-of-milestone teardown, since the relay store is disposable by design and meant to be thrown away when the parallel work finishes. `dispose` prints what it would remove and does nothing until you add `--force`, so the bare form is a safe preview. Export first if the traffic mattered.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: I registered a title and base told me to start an "inbox watcher". What is that, and can I skip it?
**A:** The watcher is a small background script, run with Claude Code's Monitor tool, that watches your relay inbox directory and wakes the session when a ping lands. It exists because relay delivery rides on hooks, which fire at a prompt or session start, so a session that goes quiet would not notice messages. `base relay arm` prints what to start it with: the Monitor tool's `description`, `command` and `timeout_ms` (1,800,000, the longest Claude Code allows), and the instruction to run `base relay arm` again whenever the Monitor reports it expired, which it does every 30 minutes. `base relay register` prints the same text when the title has no watcher. The script writes a `.watching` sentinel file on every poll, and that is the signal: `base relay board` shows a Watching column, and `base relay ping` warns the sender when the target is not watching. Without a watcher, the hooks carry one line, `relay: <title> has no inbox watcher · run base relay arm and start the Monitor it prints`, once per session and once more each time a watcher dies; they never carry the script. If your harness cannot run a background monitor, set `BASE_NO_WAKE_NUDGE` or `base config set relay.wake_nudge false` to drop the line.
<!-- v0.15.2 | verified: source -->

### Q: How do I show what a relay session is currently working on, and tag it with a project?
**A:** Write one short line to `.status` inside your relay inbox directory and re-write it whenever the work changes; the ping hub renders it on that session's card, so the live state of every session is visible at a glance without interrupting anyone. Separately, `base relay register --as <title> --project <project>` tags the session card with the project it serves. That project list is append-only: every project ever named stays on the card as a filter keyword and nothing is removed, so re-registering with a new project adds to the card rather than replacing what was there.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help|source -->

## Config, secrets, admin surfaces

### Q: How do I read and change base's configuration?
**A:** Use `base config get <section.key>` to read a value, `base config set <section.key> <value>` to write one, and `base config list` to see everything. Keys use dot-notation against `base.toml` (e.g. `devmode.enabled`, `multimodal.enabled`). Config is tiered: global `~/.base-gbl/base.toml` loads first, and a workspace's `.base/base.toml` overlays it.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help|source -->

### Q: Are there other notable config toggles besides devmode and multimodal?
**A:** Yes. `grounding.enabled` makes every prompt-time injection carry a block instructing Claude to source-verify factual claims. `graph.auto_compact` (on by default) governs whether tier graphs auto-compact at session start once they exceed `graph.compact_threshold_mb` (default 12MB), gated by `graph.compact_cooldown_hours` (default 24h) to avoid churn.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source -->

### Q: How do I install base?
**A:** Run `base install`. It builds the binary, symlinks it globally, creates `~/.base-gbl`, wires hooks into `settings.json`, and writes the manifest. Options: `--carl <path>` to migrate decisions from a `carl.json` file, `--skip-hooks` to skip wiring hooks into `settings.json`, and `--full` to register the bundled components (PAUL, SEED, SKILLSMITH) in the manifest, not just base itself.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: What does `base activate` do, and do I need it?
**A:** Nothing, and no. It used to take a key that removed attribution branding from base's output. base no longer carries that branding, so there is nothing left for the key to remove and the feature is retired. The command still parses and still exits 0 -- a provisioning script that runs `base activate $KEY` should not start failing -- and prints one line saying activation is no longer required. A manifest that already records a `token` or `source` from the old feature still loads; nothing writes those fields again.
<!-- v0.13.19 | verified: cli-help|source -->

### Q: I just installed base. What do I actually do next?
**A:** Open a new session and work normally -- there is nothing to configure first, and base learns from what you decide and correct. `base install` and `base scaffold` both print the same short message saying so. When you want more than that, `base help getting-started` covers setting a folder up as a workspace, domain triggers and rules, running more than one session on the relay, star commands, and migrating from CARL. The full documentation is at `https://docs.basemode.ai`.
<!-- v0.13.19 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I uninstall base?
**A:** Run `base uninstall`. It removes the hooks it wired into `settings.json`, removes the binary, and removes the base section from `CLAUDE.md`. By default this leaves `~/.base-gbl/` (your graph, decisions, secrets, standards) intact. See the Destructive operations section before considering `--purge`.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I store an API key or secret for base/plugins to use?
**A:** Run `base secret set` and it prompts you with echo off (masked, paste-friendly) so the value never appears in your terminal history or chat. It writes to `~/.base-gbl/.env` with file permissions `0600`. Plugins read secrets from their environment, you should never type a real secret directly into a chat session.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I see what secrets I have stored, without exposing them, and how do I remove one?
**A:** `base secret list` shows the stored key names with masked values, never the full secret. `base secret rm <key>` removes one.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I open base's web dashboard?
**A:** Run `base dashboard` (alias `base dash`). It launches the Command Center Dashboard, a local web UI, on port 3741 by default. Use `-p <PORT>` / `--port <PORT>` to choose a different port.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: What is `base standards` and what does it do?
**A:** `base standards` (alias `std`) manages context-triggered MIDAS protocol standards that get injected automatically when you edit matching files. Subcommands: `sync` (sync a MIDAS protocols.md file into `standards.toml` plus graph Standard entities), `list` (show all standards with trigger/annotation counts), `get <name>` (show a standard's full config), and `test` (dry-run the matcher against a file to see its score and what would inject).
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I add a new standard? Is there a `base standards add`?
**A:** No, there is no `add` subcommand. Standards are synced in from a MIDAS protocols markdown file via `base standards sync`, not created ad hoc through the CLI. To add a standard, edit the source protocols.md file and re-sync.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: reference -->

### Q: What is a base extension, and how do I manage them?
**A:** Extensions are drop-in plugins that add commands to base (visible via `base ext list`). Manage them with `base extension` (alias `ext`): `list` (installed extensions), `validate <file>` (check an extension manifest before installing), `install` (copy a validated TOML manifest into `extensions/`), `remove <name>`, and `run <name> [args...]` to invoke a plugin command explicitly (collision-proof).
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I install a prebuilt extension without a Rust/build toolchain?
**A:** Use `base extension add`. It fetches a plugin's prebuilt binary for your host platform from its GitHub release `[dist]` block, verifies the sha256 checksum, and unpacks/installs it, no toolchain required. If no prebuilt asset exists for your host, it falls back to a local source build.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I create a new extension from scratch?
**A:** Use `base extension scaffold` to generate a conformant, cross-platform Bun plugin. Add `--bootstrap` and it's one command: writes the files, builds it, `git init`s, and creates plus pushes a private GitHub repo, ready to develop immediately.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I check the health of base's graph?
**A:** Run `base doctor`. It diagnoses graph health across both tiers (global and workspace) using a parser-independent check, and exits with a nonzero status code when something is unhealthy, so it's scriptable in a health-check pipeline. Add `--json` for machine-readable output. Follow up with `base commands list` to confirm star commands loaded, `base project list` to confirm you're in a registered workspace and projects are visible, and `base ast list` to check code maps if relevant.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help|reference -->

### Q: What does a healthy `base doctor` report look like?
**A:** Something like: `✓ global tier - HEALTHY`, followed by the graph file path, line count, byte size, and confirmation it ends with a newline, then an overall `Verdict: HEALTHY ✓`. Each registered tier (global, and each workspace) gets its own line.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help|audit -->

### Q: base doctor says my graph is unhealthy. How do I fix it?
**A:** It depends on what doctor names. A tier that does not parse (`reason: ... (line N)`) is `base doctor --repair`: it quarantines malformed lines and atomically rewrites the good set, taking a snapshot first so nothing is lost; if a repair goes wrong, `base doctor --restore` (bare, no argument) lists available snapshots, and `base doctor --restore <snapshot>` restores the workspace graph from one (a full path to a snapshot in `~/.base-gbl/.base` restores the global graph). `--restore` takes only a backup base made, a `graph.nq.bak-*` snapshot in a tier's `.base` or a `<name>.toml.BAK-<date>-pre-<version>` an upgrade left beside a config file, and refuses any other file with the reason. Everything else doctor reports about a tier that parses, records belonging to another workspace, a correction whose text names the one record it corrects, a supersession disagreement, the legacy `[signal] max_chars`, duplicate lines and backups past `[graph] keep_backups`, is `base doctor --fix`: it prints the plan and changes nothing, and `base doctor --fix --yes` applies it. Doctor's report ends with a line naming which of those `--fix` would repair. Its count of corrections that name nothing they correct is a count, not a fault: `--fix` links the ones it can and leaves the rest as corrections, and the closing line names corrections only when `--fix` would link one. A path trigger fault and a failing hook are not `--fix`'s; their own lines name their fixes.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: What does `base doctor --fix` change, and what does it leave alone?
**A:** Per tier, in order: (1) records in a graph belonging to another workspace move out, into that workspace's own graph when it is registered (`[[workspace]]` in base.toml, the workspace you stand in, or the global tier) and its `.base` exists here, otherwise into `.base/foreign-<name>.nq` beside the graph; they move verbatim, dates and all. A "foreign" graph holding at least as many quads as the tier's own is the shape of this workspace under an earlier folder name, and it stays where it is. (2) A correction that names nothing it corrects is linked to the record it corrects when its text names exactly one note, decision or rule, by slug, by quoted text or by a decision's title (refused when that record is already superseded, is newer than the correction, or the link would close a cycle); every other one is left exactly as it is, still a correction, so it keeps its place at the top of the memory block. A second `--fix` says `nothing to do` for those. Nothing is deleted. (3) A record with status `superseded` and no edge gets the edge when another record already says it supersedes it, else its status is cleared (to `active` when nothing else is left); an edge with no status gets the status. Then each tier is compacted and keeps `[graph] keep_backups` snapshots, and `[signal] max_chars` moves to `[budget] memory_chars` when that is unset, or is removed when it is set, with every comment and other key in base.toml kept. Every graph is snapshotted before it is written. A tier that does not parse is skipped with `base doctor --repair` named first. `base graph migrate --yes` applies the same repair; it is one function.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: Where do doctor's backup snapshots go, and how many are kept?
**A:** Every repair, restore, compact, purge or fix operation snapshots the graph first, named `graph.nq.bak-<op>-<date>`, and each snapshot rotates out the oldest past `[graph] keep_backups` (default 3, per tier; it was a fixed 10 before v0.16.0). `base doctor` shows `keeps N backup(s)` per tier and warns when there are more than that; `base doctor --fix --yes` removes the oldest. Copies made by hand under another name (`graph.nq.BAK-…`, `graph.nq.torn-…`) are not base's backups and are never removed. `base doctor --restore` with no argument lists the snapshots.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->

### Q: I moved a handoff or fork from the global tier to my workspace. Why did it keep its old dates?
**A:** Because it is the same record moving, not a new one. Registering a slug with `base handoff create` or `base fork create` when another tier already holds it and this one does not copies that record's `createdAt`, `resurfaceAt` and `lastActive` (the newest copy, when several tiers hold it), so a move does not put it at the top of session start as if it were new. Registering a slug the tier you write to already holds re-points it to now, as it always has. The handoff create archives the other tier's copy (one open copy per slug); a fork create does not, so archive that one with `base fork -g archive <slug>`.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->



### Q: How do I see which standards are loaded, and what one actually contains?
**A:** `base standards list` shows every standard with its trigger and annotation counts, which is the fast way to tell whether a `base standards sync` actually landed. `base standards get <id>` prints one standard's full config. Neither writes anything, so both are safe to run any time.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I check whether a standard will fire on a given file before I trust it?
**A:** `base standards test <file>` dry-runs the matcher against that path and prints the scores plus exactly what would inject. Add `--content "<text>"` to fold extra text into the haystack, which simulates the edit payload the real hook would see, so you can test a standard that keys off file *contents* rather than just the path. Think of it as the standards equivalent of `base context "<text>"` for domains: it answers "would this actually inject?" without you having to trigger it for real.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I check an extension manifest before I install it?
**A:** `base extension validate <path>` takes the path to the extension's TOML and checks the manifest without installing anything. Run it before `base extension install`, especially on a manifest you did not write yourself, because install is a copy-into-place operation and validate is the only step that inspects what you are about to trust.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: What's the difference between `base extension install` and `base extension add`?
**A:** Different jobs despite the similar names. `base extension install <path>` takes a local, already-validated TOML manifest and copies it into `extensions/`, so it installs a manifest you already have on disk. `base extension add <path>` takes a manifest containing a `[dist]` block, then goes and fetches the actual prebuilt binary for your host from that plugin's GitHub release, verifies the sha256, and unpacks and installs it, falling back to a local source build only when no asset matches your host. Rule of thumb: `add` when you are consuming somebody's published plugin with no toolchain, `install` when you are wiring up a manifest yourself. `install` also takes `--bundle`, which copies the handler into `~/.base-gbl/plugins/<name>/` and repoints the manifest there, producing a self-contained, repo-independent install; that is the flag to use if the extension needs to survive the source folder moving or disappearing.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I create a new plugin from scratch, and what exactly does `--bootstrap` do?
**A:** `base extension scaffold <name>` writes a new, conformant, cross-platform Bun plugin, where `<name>` becomes the `base <name>` command (lowercase, hyphens fine). `--bootstrap` is the one-flag full kickoff, equivalent to `--build --git --create-repo` together: it writes the files, runs `prepare.sh` to `bun build` the binary into `bin/<name>`, runs `git init` with a first commit, then creates a private GitHub repo, wires up `origin`, and pushes. You end up with a plugin that already builds, is already versioned, and is already backed up, born cross-platform, from one command. The individual flags exist if you want less of that: `--build` only compiles, `--git` only initialises the repo, and `--create-repo` implies `--git`. Placement is controlled by `--path <dir>` (the parent directory to create `<name>-cli/` inside, defaulting to the current directory) or `--into <dir>` for an exact target folder that must be new or empty. Note that `--repo <owner/repo>` defaults to `ChristopherKahler/<name>-cli`, so pass your own `owner/repo` unless you actually want that default.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: A plugin command has the same name as a built-in base subcommand. How do I run the plugin one?
**A:** `base extension run <name> [args...]`, which is the collision-proof form. `run` addresses the plugin command explicitly by the name declared in an extension's `[[commands]]`, and everything after the name is forwarded verbatim to the handler. Drop-in plugin commands normally work as a bare `base <foo>`, but that shorthand is only unambiguous while no built-in owns the name, so `run` is both the escape hatch when one does and the safer form to use inside scripts, where you do not want a future base release to quietly shadow your plugin.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: How do I uninstall an extension?
**A:** `base extension remove <name>`, addressed by extension name rather than by path. Get the name from `base extension list`. Removing the extension stops the `base <foo>` commands it contributed from resolving.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

## Updating and versions

### Q: How do I check what version of base I'm running?
**A:** Run `base --version`. It prints the word `base` and the version baked into the running binary at build time (for example `0.13.14`), which is always accurate for the binary you are actually running, and is the source of truth for what code is running. Do not confuse it with the version recorded in `~/.base-gbl/manifest.toml`, which is a separate, independently-tracked value that can drift out of sync (see the stale-manifest bug under Known bugs).
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help|source -->

### Q: How do I check if a newer version of base is available without installing it?
**A:** Run `base update --check`. It re-validates against the remote source and reports whether a newer version exists, without installing anything. For the `base` component specifically, this compares against GitHub releases; the bundled components are checked against npm.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help|source -->

### Q: How do I actually update base to the latest version, and what is the update banner?
**A:** base checks for a newer version and can print an update banner as part of session-start injection. Run `base update` to self-update the base binary. Add `--force` to reinstall even when you are already on the latest version, or `--snooze` to dismiss the banner for 24 hours without updating (a snooze does not fix an underlying version mismatch, it only silences the banner).
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: Where does base actually get its updates from?
**A:** Public GitHub releases of the base repository, and nothing else. There is no license check, no account, and no identifier leaves the machine -- the only request is for the release list. `base` itself is checked against GitHub releases (`fetch_github_version`); the bundled components (PAUL, SEED, SKILLSMITH) are checked against their npm packages. (Before v0.13.0 this went through a license-gated channel that both sent personal data on a routine version check and pointed somewhere the release pipeline never published to, so `base update` could not deliver the releases actually being cut. That is gone.)
<!-- v0.13.19 | verified: source -->

### Q: What's in the manifest.toml file and why does it matter for updates?
**A:** `~/.base-gbl/manifest.toml` tracks, per component (base, and optionally PAUL/SEED/SKILLSMITH with `--full`), the installed version, install path, and install timestamp under `[components.<name>]`, plus an `[update_check]` section holding `last_checked`, `ttl_seconds` (default 7 days between checks), `pending_update` (the pending update string, if any), and `dismissed_until` (the `--snooze` expiry timestamp). It's the single source of truth the update banner reads from, which is exactly why a manual binary swap that doesn't touch this file causes the stale-manifest bug described under Known bugs.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source -->

### Q: I upgraded base and now it wants to defer a pile of my old handoffs and tasks. What is `base defer migrate` and do I have to run it?

**A:** Record deferral decides what is cold from a record's activity clock. On a version that predates the feature, that clock was never maintained, so on upgrade a lot of perfectly live records look untouched and would go `deferred` at the next session start. That is not data loss -- nothing is deleted and `base handoff show` or a new registration brings a record straight back -- but a screenful of your work going quiet at once is alarming, so the migration exists to stop it happening by surprise. Run `base defer migrate` to PREVIEW: it prints exactly which records would be touched and writes nothing. That is the default and there is no flag you need in order to look. When you are happy, `base defer migrate --apply` performs the reset. `base defer migrate --apply --limit <N>` touches at most N records and `base defer migrate --apply --older-than <D>` restricts it to records at least D days cold, so you can stage it rather than doing everything at once. If you do not like the result, `base defer migrate --rollback` restores every tier it wrote from the snapshot it took before writing. `base defer` on its own is just the namespace: `migrate` is the command that does the work.
<!-- v0.15.2 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: What happens when base updates itself? Do I, or my Claude, need to run anything afterwards?
**A:** No. The update swaps the binary in the background, and the first session start on the new version starts one more background process, `base hook upgrade`, which brings each tier up to the new version once and records that in the tier's `.base/upgrade.json`: the store repair `base doctor --fix --yes` makes (another workspace's records moved beside the graph, a correction linked to the one record it names, a supersession disagreement settled, compaction, old snapshots past `[graph] keep_backups`, the legacy `[signal] max_chars`), each relative path trigger written as the full path it already resolves to, and a starter star command you never edited replaced by the new version's text. Each change is backed up first. The next session start prints one `upgrade:` line per change with its undo, `base doctor --restore <backup>`, and never again. A command you edited is left as it is (if your `*base` still has the old `rule add` line, one line says so; `base commands show base --shipped` prints the current one). A `commands.toml` or `domains.toml` that is a link is never written. A repair that fails leaves what it could not repair as it was, says so once with `base doctor --fix --yes`, and is not tried again for that version. A new install has nothing to upgrade and prints nothing. `[graph] auto_migrate = false` turns all of it off.
<!-- v0.16.0 | verified: source -->
