## Known bugs (status as of v0.12.3)

### Q: The update banner keeps nagging me even though I'm already on the latest version, or base --version disagrees with what other tooling reports. What's going on and how do I fix it?
**A:** **Fixed in v0.12.0.** The bug: the update banner never compared against your actual running binary, it compared the version recorded in `~/.base-gbl/manifest.toml` under `[components.base]` against the latest remote version, and that field was only ever written by `base install` or `base update`. Swap the binary by hand (for example `cp` a new build into `~/.local/bin/base`) and the manifest went stale and nagged forever. It was self-sustaining: a non-empty `pending_update` made the banner print and return early, before the periodic check that would have recomputed it, so nothing could clear the field that was blocking the code that clears the field. `--snooze` only masked it for 24 hours via `dismissed_until`. The fix reconciles the recorded version against the running binary's `CARGO_PKG_VERSION` at session start, before anything else reads the manifest, and drops `pending_update` when the version changes, since that string was computed against the version just corrected. It is self-healing and handles rollbacks the same way.
**If you still see it** (on an older binary): correct `version` under `[components.base]` and clear `pending_update` under `[update_check]` in `~/.base-gbl/manifest.toml` by hand. `manifest.toml` is plain config rather than the graph, so hand-editing it is fine. `base --version` remains the source of truth for what code is actually running.
<!-- v0.12.3 | historical: v0.11.0 bug, fixed in v0.12.0 (745eeb8) | verified: source|audit -->

### Q: base commands import says it imported my commands, but base commands list then says "No commands configured." What happened?
**A:** **Fixed in v0.12.0.** The bug: `base commands import` wrote TOML by hand and escaped only double quotes, so any rule text containing a newline, tab, or backslash (which multi-line rules routinely do) produced an invalid basic string. The loader then discarded the parse error via an `if-let` chain with no `else` and returned an empty command list, so "Imported N command(s)" and "No commands configured" were perfectly consistent with each other and nothing told you it had failed. Re-importing appended duplicates on top of the damage, because the duplicate check parsed the already-corrupt file and got an empty set. The fix serializes the merged set through `toml::to_string_pretty`, round-trips the output back through `from_str` before writing, and refuses outright when the existing file does not parse rather than appending onto it. `base doctor` now also reports config files that exist but cannot be parsed and counts them against health, so it exits nonzero. The loader and hooks are still deliberately fail-open, because a broken file must never block a session, which is why doctor is the single place that tells you the truth.
**Practical upshot:** `base commands import` is safe to use again. If star commands ever go quiet, run `base doctor` first, it will name a corrupt config instead of leaving you guessing.
<!-- v0.12.3 | historical: v0.11.0 bug, fixed in v0.12.0 (20592ef) | verified: source|audit -->

### Q: base keeps telling me "AST graph not yet populated" / to run `base sync --ast` even though my AST map already exists and queries work fine. Why won't it stop?
**A:** **Fixed in v0.12.0.** The bug: the pre-tool-use hook's populated-check (the same check behind the grep-intercept hint) hand-joined the workspace base directory with `ast.ttl`, testing the legacy `{workspace}/.base/ast.ttl` path. Maps are written to the `{app}/.base-ast/` sidecar instead, so for any workspace mapped after the sidecar migration the check could never pass: the nag fired on every grep/find/rg Bash call and running `base sync --ast` never silenced it. Reads were never affected, because `base ast query` resolves through `find_ast_ttl` and worked throughout, which is exactly why the nag contradicted a populated `base ast list`. The fix routes the populated-check through `find_ast_ttl` too, which resolves sidecar-then-legacy, so both eras satisfy it. A second fix in the same release stops `base sync --ast` from adopting `HOME` as an app root for targets beneath it.
<!-- v0.12.3 | historical: v0.11.0 bug, fixed in v0.12.0 (ed8081f, 747d886) | verified: source|audit -->

### Q: I added a trigger to a domain and now I can't remove it. base domain list shows the domain but base domain remove says it doesn't exist. What's going on?
**A:** **Fixed in v0.14.1 (#61).** The bug, live through v0.14.0: the four `base domain` write commands did not agree on which tier they operated on. `base domain add-trigger` resolved the workspace via `find_workspace_base(cwd)` and wrote `{workspace}/.base/domains.toml`, creating both the file and the domain entry if they were missing, while `base domain create`, `base domain remove` and `base domain remove-trigger` ignored cwd and only ever touched the global `~/.base-gbl/domains.toml`. So a domain or trigger created by `add-trigger` inside a workspace could not be removed by any CLI command: `remove` and `remove-trigger` reported "Domain '<name>' not found" while `base domain list` kept showing it, because `load_domains` merges both tiers for reads. Since v0.14.1 one resolver decides the file for all four writes (the workspace file inside a registered workspace, the global file outside one or with `--global`), every write reports what it changed and in which tier, and a command that changed nothing names the tier it searched and the one it did not and exits non-zero. If you still see a not-found, you are standing in the other tier: add `--global`, or run the command from inside the workspace the domain lives in.
<!-- v0.14.2 | verified: source+binary -->

### Q: I ran a command outside a registered workspace and got back an empty result instead of an error. Is my data gone?
**A:** No, and this one is **still live in v0.12.3**. Some commands fail loudly outside a workspace (`base project list`, `base ast list`, `base task list` all error with "no .base/ directory found"). Others silently fall back to the global tier only: `base doctor` reports just the global tier, `base commands list` shows only globally-scoped commands. Worst case: `base recall --keyword <term>` can return "No results found." from the wrong cwd when the same query inside the correct workspace returns real results, so an empty answer here is indistinguishable from a genuinely empty graph.
**Fix:** `cd` into the registered workspace before trusting an empty result, or run `base scaffold` to register one. Sanity-check with `base project list` first; if that errors, treat any "empty" result from another command as suspect.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: reference -->

### Q: Why do base's hooks never show an error, even when something clearly went wrong?
**A:** **By design, still true in v0.12.3.** All five hook events (session-start, user-prompt-submit, pre-tool-use, post-tool-use, stop) fail open: any internal error is written to stderr and the process exits 0 with empty stdout, so a broken graph or a bad query never blocks your session. The tradeoff is that failures are easy to miss, because Claude Code typically doesn't surface hook stderr, so a broken hook just looks like a hook that silently had nothing to inject that turn.
**Fix:** if you suspect a hook is failing, check `hook-events.jsonl` in the relevant tier (`ts`, `hook`, `success`, `domains_matched`, etc. fields) as the audit trail, or turn on `devmode.enabled` to see per-domain firing decisions. Since v0.12.0, `base doctor` is the one surface that will not stay quiet: it reports unparseable config files and exits nonzero.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source|reference -->

### Q: Is there a full list of places where base silently swallows errors instead of telling me?
**A:** Yes, several beyond the named bugs above, and most are still live in v0.12.3: extension status injection skips silently on malformed extensions, missing query files, or query errors; session-start signal errors print to stderr and just vanish from the injected block; the stop hook's filesystem operations are fire-and-forget (`let _ = ...`), so a failed AST refresh is invisible; hook event logging is fire-and-forget; and active-path gathering returns an empty list rather than erroring when no graph is available. The command loader's `read_to_string`/`toml::from_str` chain is still fail-open by deliberate choice, but as of v0.12.0 it is no longer undiagnosable: `base doctor` reports config files that exist but cannot be parsed and counts them against health. This is a deliberate fail-open philosophy, but it means an empty or missing result is often not distinguishable from "nothing to report" without checking `base doctor`, `hook-events.jsonl`, or devmode output.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source|reference -->

### Q: Which of these bugs are actually fixed, and which are still live?
**A:** Fixed in v0.12.0: the stale-manifest update banner, the `commands import` corruption, and the AST false-nag (plus the related `sync --ast` HOME-adoption bug). Still live in v0.12.3: the `base domain` tier split, which makes a workspace-tier domain or trigger unremovable from the CLI, and `hook-events.jsonl` having no working rotation. Also still live, but as design choices rather than defects: the fail-open hook philosophy, the broad silent-error surface that follows from it, and the empty-result-outside-a-workspace gotcha. Treat the fixed group as history worth knowing, since you may still be running an older binary somewhere, and the live group as behaviour to work around.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: source|audit -->

## Destructive operations

### Q: What graph commands are safe to run freely, and which need caution?
**A:** Read-only and safe: anything named `list`, `show`, `get`, `query`, `search`, `recall`, `doctor` (without `--repair`), any `--check`, `--dry-run`, `--peek` flag, and a bare `base doctor --restore` (which only lists snapshots). Preview-by-default, meaning they show you the change but need an explicit `--yes`/`--apply`/`--force` to actually execute: `project move`, `project rename`, `project delete`, `task delete`, `milestone delete`, `graph move`, `graph purge --apply`, `relay dispose --force`. The one to actively avoid without real intent: `base uninstall --purge`, which deletes all of `~/.base-gbl/` (graph, commands, secrets) with no preview and no confirmation flag.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: reference -->

### Q: Which base commands should I be careful with, and why?
**A:** Ranked roughly by risk:
- `base uninstall --purge`: catastrophic. Deletes `~/.base-gbl/` entirely (graph, `commands.toml`, secrets `.env`, standards). No preview, no documented confirmation flag. Back up `~/.base-gbl/` first if in any doubt.
- `base project delete --force --yes`: cascade-deletes a project's tasks, milestones, and decisions. Previews unless `--yes`; refuses to run on a non-empty project without `--force`.
- `base graph purge --stale --apply`: deletes graph notes unread past a day threshold (default 21 days). Dry-run by default (needs `--apply` to actually delete); snapshots first; re-reading a note resets its clock.
- `base graph move` / `base project move`: rewrites named-graph ownership stamps across tiers. Previews unless `--yes`; backs up both tiers; atomic with rollback.
- `base task delete`: deletes a task node and its edges. Previews unless `--yes`.
- `base memory purge`: removes flat-file memories already confirmed in the graph. No preview flag.
- `base doctor --repair`: quarantines malformed graph lines. Snapshots first, so it's comparatively low-risk, but still a rewrite.
- `base decision delete --keyword <kw>`: deletes decisions matching a keyword. `--keyword` is required (no accidental delete-everything), but there's no dry-run preview shown before the delete happens.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help|reference -->

### Q: What is `base graph migrate`, and do I ever need to run it?
**A:** It gives every covered record a domain link, once per tier, and you normally never run it: it runs itself at session start and prints nothing when there is nothing to do. Run it by hand in one case — a tier whose graph was unhealthy when the hook tried is skipped, so `base doctor` keeps reporting `schema: not migrated` until you `base doctor --repair` and then `base graph migrate`. Run by hand, it also prints the store repair `base doctor --fix` plans, and `base graph migrate --yes` applies that repair too (it is the same function). Since v0.16.0 an upgrade applies that repair by itself, once, in the background (see the pair on what an update does by itself under Updating and versions). `--dry-run` shows what would be linked and by which source, and the repair plan, and writes nothing. It is idempotent the hard way: the work is recomputed from the store on every run, and the schema stamp is written inside the *same* atomic rewrite as the links, so restoring a pre-migration `.bak` correctly re-migrates and restoring a post-migration one correctly does nothing. Where each record's domain came from is reported per source — frontmatter, path-trigger, project-path, fixed, parent, or `unfiled` — so the catchall is a visible line rather than a silent remainder. `base doctor` reports each tier's `schema:` and `without a domain: N` so a migration that never ran is never invisible.
<!-- v0.13.19 | verified: cli-help -->

### Q: What does `base graph compact` / `base graph purge` / `base graph move` actually do?
**A:** `compact` dedups and canonicalizes a workspace graph in an atomic rewrite, snapshotting first. `purge --stale [--days N] [--apply]` removes notes that haven't been read in more than N days (default 21); it's a dry-run preview unless you pass `--apply`. `move` relocates a subgraph between workspace graphs, rewriting its named-graph stamp; it previews by default and requires `--yes` to actually execute, backing up both source and destination tiers with rollback support.
<!-- v0.12.3 | verified: cli-help -->

## Where base stores data

### Q: Where does each piece of base's data live on disk?
**A:** base uses two tiers that merge together when queried. The global tier lives at `~/.base-gbl/` and is loaded into every workspace: it holds the global graph (`~/.base-gbl/.base/graph.nq`), global config (`base.toml`), domain triggers (`domains.toml`), star commands (`commands.toml`), MIDAS standards (`standards.toml`), the install/update manifest (`manifest.toml`), an optional operator identity profile (`operator.toml`), and secrets (`.env`, mode 0600). The workspace tier lives inside each registered project at `{workspace}/.base/` and holds that workspace's own `graph.nq` plus config/domain/command overlays that layer on top of the global tier by name, along with handoff and fork docs and that workspace's `hook-events.jsonl`. Both tiers also carry a `changes.jsonl` written beside the graph file it describes: every successful graph write appends one JSON line to it, which is what makes a write auditable after the fact. A third location, `{app}/.base-ast/ast.ttl`, holds per-app AST code maps as a sidecar, separate from both tiers, and is never merged into the main graph.
<!-- v0.13.2 | verified: source -->

### Q: If I set up base on one machine, is any of that portable to another machine, or is it all personal to this install?
**A:** Everything under `~/.base-gbl/` (the global graph, secrets, manifest with install paths and machine-specific version state, hook-events telemetry) is machine-local and not meant to be copied wholesale to another machine, particularly `.env` (secrets) and `manifest.toml` (which records this machine's own install/update history). Workspace-tier data (`{workspace}/.base/`) travels with the project itself if the project repo is shared, though it still reflects this machine's graph state until synced. Config and domain/standards definitions (the `.toml` rule files) are the most portable piece, since they're structured, human-authored policy rather than machine state, so they can reasonably be copied or version-controlled and reapplied elsewhere. Knowledge graphs (`graph.nq`), the write log (`changes.jsonl`), telemetry (`hook-events.jsonl`), and secrets should not be treated as portable. One thing that does NOT travel even when the repo is shared: `{app}/.base-ast/` writes its own `.gitignore` containing `*`, so the code map self-ignores and is never committed. A fresh clone has no AST map until one is generated — that is by design (it regenerates on checkout), but it means you cannot count on `base ast query` working immediately after cloning someone else's repo.
<!-- v0.13.2 | verified: reference -->
